:::{#thm-spectral}
#### Spectral theorem for symmetric matrices

If $\matr{A}$ is a $p \times p$ symmetric matrix (@def-symmetric-matrix)
with real entries,
then there are a $p \times p$ orthogonal matrix $\matr{Q}$ (@def-orthogonal-matrix)
and a $p \times p$ diagonal matrix $\matr{\Lambda}$ (@def-diagonal-matrix)
with real diagonal entries $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_p$ such that

$$
\underbrace{\matr{A}}_{p \times p}
= \underbrace{\matr{Q}}_{p \times p}\,
\underbrace{\matr{\Lambda}}_{p \times p}\,
\underbrace{\tp{\matr{Q}}}_{p \times p}
$$

Each $\lambda_i$ is an eigenvalue of $\matr{A}$ (@def-eigenvalue),
and column $i$ of $\matr{Q}$ is an eigenvector of $\matr{A}$ for $\lambda_i$.
The factorization $\matr{Q}\matr{\Lambda}\tp{\matr{Q}}$
is the **eigendecomposition**, or **spectral decomposition**, of $\matr{A}$.

:::

::: notes
The proof, by induction on $p$, is outside the scope of these notes;
see @banerjee2014linear [Chapter 11, Theorem 11.27, p. 349],
which states the result in the equivalent form
$\tp{\matr{Q}}\matr{A}\matr{Q} = \matr{\Lambda}$.
The two forms are equivalent because $\tp{\matr{Q}}\matr{Q} = \matr{Q}\tp{\matr{Q}} = \matr{I}_p$:
multiply $\matr{A} = \matr{Q}\matr{\Lambda}\tp{\matr{Q}}$
by $\tp{\matr{Q}}$ on the left and by $\matr{Q}$ on the right.
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-spectral}
#### The eigendecomposition of a $2 \times 2$ symmetric matrix

For $\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$,
@exm-eigenvalue found the eigenvectors $(1, 1)$ for $3$ and $(1, -1)$ for $1$.
Each has norm $\sqrt{2}$ (@def-euclidean-norm),
so dividing each by $\sqrt{2}$ gives two orthonormal eigenvectors.
Put them in the columns of $\matr{Q}$,
and the matching eigenvalues on the diagonal of $\matr{\Lambda}$:

$$
\matr{Q} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
\qquad
\matr{\Lambda} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
$$

This $\matr{Q}$ is symmetric, so $\tp{\matr{Q}} = \matr{Q}$. Then

$$
\ba
\matr{Q}\matr{\Lambda}\tp{\matr{Q}}
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(substitute)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{2}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(collect the scalars)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{2}
\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 3 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply the first two matrices)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{2}
\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply by } \tfrac{1}{2} \text{)}
\ea
$$

which is $\matr{A}$.

:::
